terms.gloss: great-uncle on the father’s side: a grandfather’s brother
evidence: Dig. 38.10.10: patruus magnus = frāter avī (Lewis & Short)

terms.gloss: great-uncle on the mother’s side: a grandmother’s brother
evidence: Cic. Brut. 62.222; Dig. 38.10.10 (Lewis & Short: “a grandmother’s brother, great-uncle”)
terms.comment: As with uncles, Latin keeps the two sides apart: the grandfather’s brother is patruus magnus, the grandmother’s brother avunculus magnus. In the jurists major is one generation further up (great-great-uncle).

terms.gloss: great-uncle in the historians; in the jurists, a great-great-uncle
evidence: Vell. 2.59; Suet. Aug. 7; Suet. Claud. 3 (Lewis & Short: “in the histt. sometimes avunculus major = avunculus magnus”)
terms.comment: Traupman’s word for great-uncle. The jurists use it of the great-grandmother’s brother, a great-great-uncle, but the historians use it of the grandmother’s brother (Lewis & Short), so it has ancient warrant; avunculus magnus is the unambiguous term.

evidence: Tac. A. 12.22; Dig. 38.10.10: patruus major = frāter proavī (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Lewis & Short gives it only as the great-grandfather’s brother, a great-great-uncle, in Tacitus and the jurists; the great-uncle on the father’s side is patruus magnus.

sources: Lewis & Short: patruus · Lewis & Short: avunculus
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 24, checked against the searchable text of the book.: p. 323.
